title: The Self and the Listener
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett reads Lew Welch's poem "Small Sentence to Drive Yourself Sane" and Barry Magid's passage comparing just sitting to looking in a mirror. Nomon then turns to the fourteenth-century teacher Basui and his question "Who hears?", found in Nelson Foster's The Roaring Stream. In Basui's recorded exchange, skeptical listeners ask where the practice comes from, and Basui points to the Shurangama Sutra, where Manjushri tells Ananda to listen to the listener. Nomon sets this beside a personal story: five years of counting breaths, then counting backward at a teacher's suggestion, then the question "What is it?" from Norman. The evening closes on Welch's line "So, it's all come to this," offered for moments of tangling up in self-improvement.

sentences.text: Good evening, everybody.
A poem from Lew Welch that Bob Rose shared with us last night, or last week, I mean.
It's called "Small Sentence to Drive Yourself Sane."

*The next time you are doing something absolutely ordinary, or even better, the next time you are doing something absolutely necessary, such as pissing, or making love, or washing the dishes, or the baby, or yourself, or the room, say to yourself, "So, it's all come to this."*
So it's all come to this.
It's really kind of always true right now.
So it's all come to this.
So it's all come to this.
These five people are the perfect people to be here.
Tonight, that's what it's come to.
The next moment, it's come to something else.
That's the thing.
Where we get stuck might be that we think it's all come to this, and that we're stuck with it.
But actually, it's all come to this.
And now it's all come to this.
So that's a great little poem.
I've never heard that before.
I know just a little bit about Lew Welch.
Unfortunately, we didn't record Bob Rose's talk, his student talk, kind of informal.
I didn't want him to feel pressured by the little thing. [unclear: "A little light sucking up his words"], you know.
And then they go on the internet and all that.
But that was the gist of it.
So it's all come to this.
So, a few findings from the world to share tonight.
Somehow this will all tie together.
Here's a short piece from a Zen teacher named Barry Magid.
This is maybe not quite directly on the topic of our first Western Zen ancestors that we've been looking at, which we'll look at in a lot more detail in the practice period.
But everybody ties in somehow.
Barry was a student of Joko Beck.
There are a couple of wonderful books in the library of Joko Beck's short Dharma talks.
And Joko Beck was a student of Taizan Maezumi Roshi, who is one of the teachers that we'll look at in the practice period.
So Barry Magid, who lives in New York, I think, and is also a psychotherapist, is like the grandson of Maezumi Roshi.
He wrote:
*Imagine sitting down in front of a mirror.
Your face automatically appears.
There's no effort required.
The mirror is doing all the work.
You can't do it right or wrong.*
In other words, you're there in front of the mirror.
There's no way to do your reflection wrong.
There's no way to do your reflection right.
*Zen Buddhist practice of just sitting is like that.
When we sit, our mind automatically begins to display itself to us, just like the reflection.
Our practice is to observe and experience what appears moment after moment.
Of course, just as when we look in a real mirror, things don't stay that simple for long.
We notice how our faces or our bodies look in the mirror, and we immediately have an emotional reaction and form judgments about what we are.

Rainer Maria Rilke wrote that Paul Cezanne was capable of painting a self-portrait with utter objectivity, of looking at his own face with no more reaction than, quote, a dog seeing itself in a mirror and thinking, "Look, there's a dog."
But for the rest of us, it's not so easy to simply observe who we are.
Looking in the mirror, we're tempted to use it as a makeup mirror to touch up parts of our self-image that we don't like.
To me, if we were like Cezanne, we could look in the mirror and say, "Oh, look, there's a person.
That's interesting."
Our minds are never what we want them to be.
That's part of why we're uncomfortable with ourselves as we are.
The greatest dualism we face is the split between who we are and who we think we ought to be.
Sometimes that gap fuels our aspiration to follow the Buddha's teachings.
Sometimes it simply fuels our self-hatred, and all too often we confuse these two notions of self entirely.*
All too often we confuse these two notions of self entirely.
So the notion of the self that we actually see in the mirror, and the self that we superimpose on that image, of who we think we should be or shouldn't be.
*Just sitting means sitting still with all these aspects of our self, all the aspects that we came to Buddhist practice in order to avoid or change.
Our restlessness, our anxiety, our fear, our anger, our wandering mind.
Our practice is just to watch, to just feel.
We watch our minds think.
Minds think.
There's no problem.
Minds just do what they do.
Ordinarily we get caught up in the content of our thoughts.
But when we just sit,* just sit is a particular meaning there, *when we just sit, we observe ourselves just thinking.
Our body's most basic activity is breathing.
No matter what else is going on, we are breathing.
So we sit and we breathe.
And we feel the sensation of our breath in our body.
Often there's tension or even pain somewhere in our bodies as well.
We sit and feel that too.
And we keep breathing.
Whatever thoughts come, come.
Whatever feelings come, come.
We're not sitting there to fight off our thoughts or try to make ourselves stop thinking.
When we sit, we realize how unwilling we are to leave anything about our self alone.*
That's worth noticing in that sentence.
When we sit we notice how unwilling we are to leave anything about ourselves alone.
*We turn our lives into one endless self-improvement project.
All too often what we call meditation or spirituality is simply incorporated into our obsession with self-criticism and self-improvement.

I've encountered many students who have attempted to use meditation in order to perform a kind of spiritual lobotomy on themselves, trying to excise once and for all their anger, their fear, their sexuality, whatever it is.
We have to sit with our resistance to feeling whole.* Sit with our resistance to feeling whole.
*To feeling all those painful and messy parts of ourselves.
Just sitting means just that.
That "just" endlessly goes against the grain of our need to fix, transform, and improve.
The paradox of our practice is that the most effective way of transformation is to leave ourselves alone.
The more we let everything be just what it is, the more we relax.
The more we relax into an open attentive awareness of one moment after another.
Just sitting leaves everything just as it is.*
And so it's come to this.
Just this, just this.
So that's a pretty interesting explication about just sitting.
So this is modern.
I don't know when he wrote this, a couple of years ago.
And so this little talk, I guess, is inspired by Bob.
I bet he's not here, but maybe he'll listen to this.

Bob was telling us that a great book that he's appreciated for a long time in his studies is called *The Roaring Stream*, a Zen reader put together by Nelson Foster, a Zen teacher, and his friend Jack Shoemaker.
I kind of flipped through this one time, probably in the Tassajara library actually, and I never really studied it.
So I got a hold of it and I was reading it this morning.
I came across an interesting thing from a Japanese Zen teacher named Basui, fourteenth century.
And Basui, how does he fit into all these stories we've been hearing?
Basui was a student of Gasan Josaki, and Gasan Josaki was a student of Keizan.
Maybe you remember Taras' talk about Keizan.
Talus' talk
Keizan was a couple of generations after Dogen.
But that talk made the interesting point that Keizan was connected directly to Dogen through his mother and his grandmother.
So Basui is like the Dharma grandson of Keizan.
And anyway, Basui, like many of the Zen teachers who get celebrated later, was a bit of an outsider.
He didn't like the big Zen places in the capital.
There must have been many hundreds and thousands of Zen monks and teachers keeping all those places going that we never hear about anymore.
But the outsiders who were able to just ride on their backs and do something else, we hear about.
Anyway, he wandered around the countryside and had small temples, although in the end, I guess, he was a pretty popular teacher.
But like Keizan and his teacher, Gasan Josaki, he was really interested in Zen practice for non-monastics, for ordinary people.
So there's a little thread of that through Soto Zen, which is quite beautiful.
It's a pretty small thread, but a really beautiful thing.
And anyway, Barry Magid was advocating the practice of just sitting, and Basui advocated the practice of working with a question.
Sitting with a question.
And the way Nelson Foster writes it in the introduction:
*Basui's outsider status entailed more than just distance from the Buddhist establishment.
He was apparently by nature a critic and chose to do his teaching in a manner entirely his own.

Eschewing both the Rinzai approach to koan study, which he evidently found formulaic, and the Soto approach, which he deemed merely intellectual, Basui counseled his students to dwell single-mindedly on the question, "Who is the master of hearing this sound?"*
That's how they translate his question from the Japanese.
Who is the master of hearing this sound?
I think maybe for our purposes we might simplify that a little bit.
That's a long expression.
To something like, who hears?
Who hears?
So to sit and be open to sound, really listening to sound, and working with this question, who hears?
Who hears?
So kind of like Barry Magid: who is this in the mirror?
What is this mind?
What is this life?
So he had this, oh, that's the sole practice he advocated.
Who hears?
A restatement of his own natural koan.
We said earlier in his enlightenment story, he kind of came up with his own koans.
So this was connected to what he discovered in his own practice.
Presumably, Barry Magid really appreciated, in the years with his teacher and beyond, a sense of just sitting without any sort of deliberate intervention in the mind.
So Nelson Foster goes on writing about Basui:
*In his writings and oral record, he returns again and again to this problem, pressing it on his audiences with a fervency and creativity striking even in translation six centuries later.
Questions from his listeners betray incredulity and even skepticism that the way could be this simple and this uniform for one and all.
But Basui staunchly defends his method.

When he does allude to cases from classic texts, he takes them up mainly to test his students and to drive them off of superficial understandings in the interest of achieving thoroughgoing realization.
In the process, he demonstrates an impressive command of koans, leaving little doubt as to the depths of his studies.*
So he knew all this other stuff, but he didn't have his students work on it directly.
And then a little more about his story, and then I'll read you a little bit of what he actually said.

*Though he always referred to his temple as a hermitage and is remembered as a kind of solo outsider, he actually spent his last ten years amid a large crowd of disciples, as many as a thousand at a time.
And a strong populist streak is apparent in his words.

Like the Pure Land and Nichiren teachers who had attracted a large public during the preceding two centuries, he preached a path of liberation accessible to all, and in demystifying enlightenment, he located it within the reach of anyone who undertook this practice earnestly and energetically.
Gender, ordination, education, and social status mattered not at all.*
And he wanted all his writing to be published in ordinary Japanese too, not weird Chinese phrases.
What's cool about his record is that he, or maybe his students, recorded the question and answer.
Here's a question and answer from the fourteenth century.
Presumably he's giving a big talk, and lots of people from the town and all around are there.
And he's been talking about this practice of who hears.
*Question.

Master, you said earlier that the true teaching of the Buddhas and ancestors is nothing other than pointing directly to people's minds and showing them that seeing into their own nature is Buddhahood.
Now you talk neither of mind nor of nature.
You just say we should look at that which listens to the Dharma.
What does this mean?*
*Basui: This is the true key to understanding your own nature directly.*
*Question.
Is this phrase, "that which hears the Dharma," who hears, an expedient means created by you, master?
Or is it from the sayings of Buddhas and ancestors?*
That's an important question.
Where did this come from?
What's the providence?
*Basui: It is neither my expedient means nor is it from the sayings of the Buddhas and ancestors.*
Good dodge.
*It is the innate perfection of all people.
It's the innate perfection of all people.
The exquisite gate of emancipation of the Buddhas and ancestors.*
So it's natural and organic.
*Question.
It is said that that which has not appeared in the texts from ancient times is no subject for discussion by wise people.
If this has never appeared in the sayings of the Buddhas and ancestors, who would believe it?*
Who would believe it unquestioningly?
So this is interesting.
And what's interesting to me is that maybe he or his students, whoever allowed this in the record, so he's really getting criticized.
Who would believe this?
Bossui: *There are no words for the way.
There are no words for the way.
That's why it's independent of the sayings of Buddhas and ancestors.
Though it is innate to all people, words are used to express it.
So how could it be contrary to the writings of the Buddhas and ancestors?* This is getting a little more tactical.
There are no words for the way, so this is beyond words.
That's why it's independent of the sayings of Buddhas and ancestors.
How we practice is not dependent on those words.
*Though it is innate to all people, words are used to express it.* So we have to use words.

*So how could it be contrary to the writings of the Buddhas and ancestors?* Question: *If that is so, then which sutra concurs with this teaching?* I don't know if it was the same guy all the time or different people.
Well, it wasn't recorded.
It's a very traditionalist people out there.
Yeah, yeah.
Wait a minute.
He keeps teaching though.
It doesn't bother him.
So Bossui answers: *At the Shuram Gama meeting.* That means there's a sutra called the Shuram Gama Sutra, which we now know is apocryphal and written in China.
*At the Shuram Gama meeting, there were many sages practicing and entering the gate.* There's a scene in the sutra with many important teachers and monks practicing different ways.
*There were 25 perfections in all.
At the Shuram Gama meeting, where many sages practiced and entered the gate, there were 25 perfections in all.*
So 25 practices are described.
It's a really long sutra.
*The one gate, the so-called one who hears the Dharma,* just mentioned, my practice of who hears, *was the perfection achieved by the Bodhisattva Kanan.* Kanan is a Japanese name for Avalokiteshvara.
*The Bodhisattva Manjushri,* this one, Bodhisattva Wisdom, *asked by the world-honored one,* the Buddha, *to comment on this gate, to comment on hearing, praised it, and called it the primary gate.*
So many different Bodhisattvas and Buddhas are quoted in the sutra about how they practice.
Avalokiteshvara says, I practice by hearing the world, hearing the Dharma.
One of the names of Avalokiteshvara is the one who hears the world, or hears the cries of the world, Kanzeon.
Then Manjushri, who stands for wisdom, so if he says it's good, that's really good, is asked by the Buddha to comment, and he says that's good, that's really good, that's a primary practice.
Here's where it comes back to us.
*At this point, Manjushri said to Ananda.* Do you remember who Ananda is?
He's the cousin and assistant of the Buddha, who famously remembered all the teachings, but somehow didn't quite get it.
He remembered everything word for word, but he didn't really deeply understand, until later on he does.

*So at one point, Manjushri said to Ananda, "Though you have heard all the secret teachings of Buddhas, as countless as atoms, you have yet to eliminate the flow of desire, and thus have been mistakenly holding on to all you have heard.
Rather than entertaining what you have heard from the many Buddhas, why don't you listen to the listener?"*
Let's read that again.
This is Manjushri criticizing Ananda, and therefore criticizing us, because we're Ananda, basically.
We find that we've been listening to these teachings, we've been practicing, and we don't get it.

So Manjushri says to Ananda, *Though you have heard all the secret teachings of Buddhas, countless as atoms, and have yet to eliminate the flow of desire,* you have yet to eliminate the flow of desire, you're still kind of grabby, kind of clinging, *and thus you have been mistakenly holding on to all you have heard.* That's powerful, because what Ananda's been holding on to is the teachings of the Buddha.
So he's saying, that's a mistake, let go of that.
*Rather than entertaining what you have heard from the many Buddhas, why don't you listen to the listener?* Who hears?
So who is that in the mirror?
Who is it that's experiencing vision, or thought, or sound?
Another great thing in the Zen tradition, which is brought up by both these teachers, is the power of just sticking to one practice.
Dogen writes about this.
I don't know if you've noticed, in the two pieces that we chant by Dogen, the Fukan, the Zen-gi, and the Genjokoan, he more or less says, to practice one practice is complete.
Just totally focus on one practice, and just let go of everything.
It's a complete practice.
This is a little strange to us, because we believe there's something wrong with us, and we want to improve.
Barry Magid was criticizing, and as Bossui was quoting and criticizing, it would seem like we would need different practices, maybe a whole variety, like we would want to be skillful.
We would have this practice for this problem, and this practice for that problem.
Sometimes meditation, and mindfulness especially, get talked about like a toolbox, right?
You need different tools to solve your different problems.
So how could it be that only one practice would be enough?
The other great advantage and disadvantage we have, living in this modern age, is that we have access to so many different practices.

You can watch on YouTube lectures of what used to be secret Tibetan practices that you would never be able to learn in a million years, unless you did years of preliminary practices, were in the right place at the right time, probably were male, and probably Tibetan or something.
So now we have access to all these practices, and yet we have this deep thought in Zen that just doing one practice completely and wholeheartedly is enough.
I think what's great about that thought is that it requires a lot of faith.
It requires a lot of faith that we don't have to figure this out.
Selecting which practice and which technique and how to do it implies a certain obligation to us to be really smart, really crafty, and really skillful.
Maybe this whole process is actually undermined by that very way of thinking, trying to fix the guy in the mirror, trying to do it just right.
When I first started practicing in the 80s, I was told at the introductory meeting, count your breath.
We were a little group of us, and we were instructed to count our breaths.
Nobody ever told me anything else, so that's all I did.
I did go to Dokusan, but maybe I never asked about that, or maybe they didn't have any other practices then, or maybe they thought I should just keep practicing.
I have no idea, actually.
For the first five years of my practice, and I was pretty into it, I just did breath counting, one to ten, and one, two.
That's all I did.
I tried to do it during the day too, not just during meditation, just all the time.
Eventually I found myself at Tassajara during the practice period there, which is our big deal place, a place of deep practice.
It occurred to me for the first time: is this all there is?
Just this one?
I felt like I was getting kind of automatic or kind of stale.
I could do it, more or less.
The mind would wander off, but in the average period, I could do quite a bit of counting.
I've told you this story before.
I went to the teacher, and I said, this breath counting thing seemed a little stale.
Was there some other practice I should be doing?
And she said, huh, kind of stale, kind of automatic?
I said, yeah, I just kind of automatically can count one, two, three, four.
And she said, well, it would probably be less automatic if you counted backwards.
So then I started counting backwards from ten down to one.
It kind of reinvigorated it, and made me feel a little more fresh.
I did that for another three years.
Then finally I went to Norman, I talked about this, and maybe I just never had asked, I don't know.
He said, well, why don't you forget about counting?
Maybe that's enough counting.
And he gave me a question to work with.
Not the question who hears, but what is it?
What is it?
So I think it might be skillful to eventually change a practice, but I think it's really helpful to us.

It's not that the counting brought me any particular insight or anything like that, maybe some support and a certain kind of stability, but there's a kind of renunciation baked into this idea of really sticking to one practice, whether you're tired of it, whether you love it, whether you're excited by it, whether you read about it in an important book, whether you hate it.
Just sticking with one practice for quite a while.
Eventually maybe a teacher can see, okay, maybe that's enough, you can do another practice.
So then I could do this practice of what is it, what is it?
What is it?
Just this one question.
I never thought of other questions or tweaked it or improved it.
Just what is it?
Sometimes the words just fall away.
It's just sort of a feeling question.
Other people in our family have worked with different questions.
It's good to receive the question from the teacher, I think, and not just make up your own.
Not that one is necessarily better than the other.
I don't know that what is it is any better or worse than who hears, or just this, which is a question Bob mentioned last week that he's worked with for a long time.
Then maybe after a while, five years, ten, that's enough of that.
Then maybe just sitting, as Barry Magid described.

Another possible practice for us is just following the breath with no words, without trying to figure out the breath, just being with the breath, just a fullness of awareness of breath and body and breath and body.
That's more or less our menu, I think.
Pretty simple menu: counting, following, working with a phrase, just sitting.

All this is supported and enlivened by studying these teachings, learning about these different ancestors, being curious about who they were and what this was for them, and being curious in the middle of our life: what is this, what is this life of mine?
But I think it's good that we have a tradition that is not that clever about which practices to do.
It has this deep faith that just doing one practice wholeheartedly, steadily, over time, just showing up, in other words, is enough.

That may, little by little, free us from some of these layers of desire that Manjushri is criticizing Ananda for in the story that Bossui quotes: this desire to understand it all, to figure it all out, to do it the right way, to remember everything.
It's kind of just feeding the beast, I think.
I think that's what is great about Zen, that it short circuits this whole process by sticking to very simple practices with a lot of faith and a long time.
And the central emphasis is just showing up.
Just showing up is enough.
I appreciate the five of us for doing that practice, just showing up.
Everyone else is just showing up somewhere else, right?
So that's okay.
They're doing their practice too.
I don't know if it makes it more magical or more special to do this for a long time, and whether this is even a long time, maybe it's a short time.
But it's kind of great.
I appreciate that somebody always shows up.
For nearly 25 years now, somebody shows up every week for Zen Buddhist practice in Bellingham.
Simply sitting.
Simply counting, simply following the breath.
Noticing when the mind gets caught in some crazy pattern, which always has some level of desire in it for things to be somehow other than the way they are.
If we get all tangled up in trying to be someone better or different or more improved, maybe we can remember Lew Welch's advice in that moment.
Either we're calm and happy and enjoying a moment, or we're tangled up and upset and confused and it all seems hopeless.
We can also just remind ourselves: so, it's all come to this, okay?
Thanks very much.
